# Spring Boot Web Application using Container Runtime Hardening

This runbook uses the same Spring Boot quote application as the
[container image hygiene](../container-image-hygiene-spring-boot/) example. Here
the focus is what the running process can change. A working image alone does not
establish whether the application needs root privileges, whether it can
overwrite packaged files, or where it stores temporary files and diagnostic
evidence.

Build one image, then change its runtime settings without rebuilding it. Compare
writable and read-only execution, provide only the writable paths needed by the
application, and preserve a Flight Recorder recording after removing the
container. The application uses an in-memory H2 database and writes its logs to
standard output. It does not need a writable database directory or a file-log
directory.

This focused example does not cover every aspect of running Java in containers.
See the [all-in-one Spring Boot example](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md)
for a more holistic example that combines the workshop techniques. Image
digests, SBOMs and vulnerability scans belong to the
[container image hygiene example](../container-image-hygiene-spring-boot/README.md).

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- verify the declared and effective non-root identity;
- compare filesystem writes with and without `--read-only`;
- run the quote application with bounded temporary storage and restricted
  privileges; and
- save and retrieve diagnostic evidence after removing the application
  container.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with a running Linux
  container engine. Docker Desktop provides this on macOS and Windows.

- `curl`, used to verify the quote endpoint.

- `jq`, used to format the quote response.

### Oracle Container Registry access

Before pulling an Oracle Java base image, sign in to Oracle Container Registry
and accept the terms for the
[Oracle Java JDK repository](https://container-registry.oracle.com/ords/ocr/ba/java/jdk).

1. Accept the Oracle Container Registry terms.

2. Authenticate your container engine with your own Oracle Container Registry
   username and authentication token.

   Pass the token through standard input so it is neither recorded in shell
   history nor copied into the project or image layers. If you use Podman, use
   its equivalent `login --password-stdin` command.

   ```shell
   docker login container-registry.oracle.com \
     --username 'ALBERT.ATTARD@ORACLE.COM' \
     --password-stdin < ~/.ocr/auth-token
   ```

   This should print the login succeeded message.

   ```
   Login Succeeded!
   ```

3. Verify that the container engine can pull and run the Oracle Java JDK image.

   ```shell
   docker run --rm 'container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' java --version
   ```

   Docker pulls the image if necessary, then prints the Java runtime version.

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   ```

## The artefacts to inspect

The executable Spring Boot JAR is the controlled input throughout the
walkthrough. The Dockerfile keeps the JAR owned by root and readable by the
application, then starts Java as the numeric user and group `10001:10001`. A
numeric identity does not require a user-management tool or an account entry in
the image.

The application cannot write to its JAR through ordinary file permissions. The
read-only root filesystem adds a separate restriction over the image filesystem.
Neither decision grants write access to a mounted volume automatically: the
mount must also have suitable ownership and permissions.

The Dockerfile includes `/diagnostics` as a mount point. It does not declare a
`VOLUME`, so the deployment must explicitly provide writable storage there.
`--read-only`, temporary storage and capabilities are runtime settings rather
than Dockerfile instructions.

```dockerfile
FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
WORKDIR "/opt/app"

# The application user cannot write here unless the deployment mounts
# writable storage with suitable ownership and permissions.
RUN mkdir "/diagnostics" && chmod 0755 "/diagnostics"

# Keep application files owned by root and readable by the application user.
ARG JAR_FILE="./target/container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot-*.jar"
COPY --chown=0:0 --chmod=0444 ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

USER 10001:10001

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

The `.dockerignore` file provides an additional build-time guardrail. Docker
applies it on every build to exclude unrelated files from the build context,
including source code, documentation and other build output, while allowing the
executable JAR under `target/`. It does not change the privileges or filesystem
restrictions of the running container.

The Dockerfile already copies only the application JAR, so removing
`.dockerignore` would leave this image’s contents and runtime behaviour
unchanged. Keeping it limits what a future broader `COPY` instruction could
include accidentally. Files in the build context are available to the builder;
they become part of the image only when a build instruction includes them. See
[Docker’s build context documentation](https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/context/#dockerignore-files)
for the exclusion rules.

```text
**
!containers/
!containers/Dockerfile-non-root
!target/
!target/container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot-*.jar
```

## Build the application

Run the following commands from this example directory. Build the application
once and reuse its executable JAR for every container step. The copied tests
verify the same quote service, repository and controller as the image hygiene
example.

1. Build and test the application.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. (*Optional*) Run the packaged application

   This starts the JAR outside a container. A successful endpoint response
   establishes that the application artefact works before its runtime layout is
   changed by container packaging.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote. A JSON response confirms that the packaged service is
   running and can serve its endpoint.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Isaac Newton",
     "id": 84,
     "quote": "Live your life as an Exclamation rather than an Explanation."
   }
   ```

   Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Guided walkthrough

Run the following sections from this example directory. Each step uses the same
application image, so the observations show the effect of runtime settings
rather than changes to the application or its packaging.

First, verify the non-root identity and compare filesystem writes with and
without a read-only root filesystem. Then provide explicit writable storage for
temporary files and diagnostic output, confirm that the application still serves
requests, and retrieve a JFR recording after removing its container.

Follow the commands for your container engine. Docker and Podman differ in their
handling of temporary mounts and volume options, so replacing the command name
alone is insufficient.

### Verify the runtime identity

The same image is used for both filesystem configurations. This isolates the
runtime restrictions from application packaging and base-image changes.

1. Build the non-root image.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
     --tag 'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
     .
   ```

2. Inspect the runtime user declared by the image.

   This reads the image configuration without starting a container.

   ```shell
   docker image inspect 'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
     --format 'declared user={{.Config.User}}'
   ```

   The image declares user and group `10001:10001` as its default runtime
   identity.

   ```
   declared user=10001:10001
   ```

3. Verify the effective identity of a started process.

   Override the application entrypoint with `id` to check which user and group
   the container runtime actually applies.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --entrypoint id \
     'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root'
   ```

   The process runs with UID 10001 and GID 10001, confirming that the runtime
   applies the image’s declared non-root identity.

   ```
   uid=10001(10001) gid=10001(10001) groups=10001(10001)
   ```

### Compare filesystem writes

Non-root execution and a read-only root filesystem solve different problems. A
non-root process can still write to directories that grant it permission, such
as the image’s `/tmp`. A read-only root filesystem prevents those
image-filesystem writes too.

1. Verify that the non-root user can write a temporary file with normal
   execution. This command uses a shell to inspect the filesystem instead of
   starting Java.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --entrypoint sh \
     'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
     -c 'touch /tmp/workshop-write-test && echo "Temporary write succeeded"'
   ```

   The image filesystem is writable at `/tmp` under normal execution.

   ```
   Temporary write succeeded
   ```

2. Repeat the same write with a read-only root filesystem.

   Use the command for your container engine. Docker’s `--read-only` leaves
   `/tmp` within the read-only root filesystem. Podman provides writable
   temporary mounts by default, so its command also uses
   `--read-only-tmpfs=false` to disable them.

   Both commands attempt the same write without providing writable storage
   at `/tmp`. The non-zero exit status is intentional: Sociable Weaver checks
   for exit code 1 and the read-only filesystem error, then continues the
   walkthrough.

   - Docker

     ```shell
     docker run \
       --rm \
       --read-only \
       --entrypoint sh \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
       -c 'touch /tmp/workshop-write-test' 2>&1
     ```

   - Podman

     ```shell
     podman run \
       --rm \
       --read-only \
       --read-only-tmpfs=false \
       --entrypoint sh \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
       -c 'touch /tmp/workshop-write-test' 2>&1
     ```

     The temporary write fails because `/tmp` is part of the read-only root
     filesystem.

     ```
     touch: cannot touch '/tmp/workshop-write-test': Read-only file system
     ```

The shell check provides a deterministic observation without depending on a
particular Spring Boot startup failure. Java and frameworks may need temporary
files during startup or only when handling a later request. Changing
`java.io.tmpdir` selects a location for Java APIs that use it; it does not
create writable storage or relocate every native JVM temporary file.

### Provide explicit writable storage

Use `/tmp` for disposable files and `/diagnostics` for evidence that should
survive container removal. Keep the packaged runtime and application read-only.

| Content                                                        | Storage in this example                  |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Java runtime and application JAR                               | Read-only image filesystem               |
| Framework temporary files, JVM attach files and JFR repository | Bounded `/tmp` tmpfs                     |
| Exported JFR recording                                         | Writable Docker volume at `/diagnostics` |
| Application logs                                               | Standard output and error                |

A tmpfs is temporary storage backed by memory and can use swap if the host
permits it. Its contents disappear when the container stops. Budget it alongside
the JVM heap and other container memory. The limits below are workshop settings
rather than a sizing recommendation. Prepared CDS or AOT caches can stay in the
read-only image when the JVM only consumes them. Cache generation needs writable
storage.

1. Create a fresh Docker volume and record its generated name.

   Using an explicit, fresh name avoids changing an existing volume and prevents
   automatic removal with a setup container. Only this new volume is removed
   during cleanup.

   ```shell
   docker volume create "runtime-hardening-$(date +%s)-$$" > './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'
   ```

   A fresh Docker volume created with default settings normally has a root-owned
   directory. If the application runs as a non-root user, it may therefore lack
   permission to create files in that directory. Prepare the volume by assigning
   ownership to the application’s user ID and setting suitable permissions
   before using it. This preparation is normally needed only once per volume,
   provided the application’s user ID and the directory permissions remain
   unchanged.

2. Prepare the volume so the application running as non-root can save diagnostic
   files.

   The Java process runs as user ID (UID) 10001 and group ID (GID) 10001. A
   fresh volume may belong to root, leaving the application unable to create
   files in it. Mounting the volume makes it accessible inside the container,
   but does not by itself grant the application write permission.

   Start a temporary setup container as root (`--user 0:0`) and mount the
   volume at `/diagnostics`. The shell command changes that directory’s owner
   and group to `10001:10001`, then applies permissions `0700`. These give the
   owner permission to read, write and traverse the directory, while denying
   ordinary access to other users.

   The setup container exits and is removed, but the named volume retains its
   ownership and permissions. The application can then use it without running as
   root. This preparation is normally needed only once per volume, provided the
   application’s UID and the directory permissions remain unchanged. Rebuilding
   the image with updated application code does not require preparing the same
   volume again.

   Use one of the following commands for your container engine. Both perform the
   same preparation, but Docker uses `volume-nocopy` with `--mount`, whereas
   Podman uses `:nocopy` with `--volume`. These options prevent copying the
   image directory into the volume. Podman also needs `--read-only-tmpfs=false`
   to disable its automatic writable temporary mounts. The root filesystem stays
   read-only, while the diagnostic volume remains writable.

   - Docker

     ```shell
     docker run \
       --rm \
       --read-only \
       --user 0:0 \
       --entrypoint sh \
       --mount "type=volume,source=$(cat './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'),target=/diagnostics,volume-nocopy" \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
       -c 'chown 10001:10001 /diagnostics && chmod 0700 /diagnostics'
     ```

   - Podman

     ```shell
     podman run \
       --rm \
       --read-only \
       --read-only-tmpfs=false \
       --user 0:0 \
       --entrypoint sh \
       --volume "$(cat './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'):/diagnostics:nocopy" \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
       -c 'chown 10001:10001 /diagnostics && chmod 0700 /diagnostics'
     ```

3. Start the application with restricted privileges and explicit writable
   storage.

   The quote service needs to serve HTTP requests and write diagnostic files. It
   does not need to change file ownership, bypass ordinary file permissions or
   create raw network packets. `--cap-drop=ALL` removes Linux capabilities that
   grant these privileged operations. `no-new-privileges` also prevents gaining
   privileges through mechanisms such as setuid executables. These restrictions
   reduce the potential damage if an attacker executes code through the
   application, but do not prevent a compromise or misuse of its legitimate
   access.

   The application runs as the image’s non-root user with a read-only root
   filesystem. Provide a writable `/tmp` for temporary files and mount the
   prepared diagnostic volume at `/diagnostics` for saved recordings. The
   temporary directory uses mode `1777`, allowing users to create files while
   restricting deletion of other users’ files through the sticky bit.

   Limit `/tmp` to 128 MiB, container memory to 512 MiB and the Java heap to
   256 MiB. Temporary storage and other JVM memory must fit alongside the heap
   within the container limit. These are workshop settings rather than sizing
   recommendations. Start a JFR recording with the JVM and configure its maximum
   retained recording size as 32 MiB.

   Use the variant for your container engine. Both apply the same intended
   restrictions. By default, Podman keeps `/tmp`, `/run` and `/var/tmp` writable
   even with `--read-only`. Adding `--read-only-tmpfs=false` disables those
   automatic writable mounts. We then use `--tmpfs /tmp:...` to make only `/tmp`
   writable among those temporary directories, with the size and permissions
   specified in the command.

   Docker mounts the diagnostic volume using `--mount` with `volume-nocopy`;
   Podman uses `--volume` with `:nocopy`. These options prevent copying the
   image directory into the prepared volume.

   This runbook selects Docker on macOS and Podman on Linux to match the
   workshop environments. You do not need both engines installed.

   Publish container port 8080 on host port 8080, which must be available. The
   quote endpoint is accessible at `http://localhost:8080/quote/random`. This
   mapping binds to all host network interfaces. Name the container
   `container-runtime-hardening` so later steps can inspect it and collect
   diagnostic evidence. The name must be available in the selected engine;
   remove any leftover container from a previous run before starting again.

   - Docker

     ```shell
     docker run \
       --detach \
       --name 'container-runtime-hardening' \
       --read-only \
       --cap-drop=ALL \
       --security-opt=no-new-privileges \
       --memory=512m \
       --tmpfs /tmp:rw,nosuid,nodev,size=128m,mode=1777 \
       --mount "type=volume,source=$(cat './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'),target=/diagnostics,volume-nocopy" \
       --publish 8080:8080 \
       --env 'JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS=-Xmx256m -XX:StartFlightRecording=name=demo,settings=default,maxsize=32m' \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root'
     ```

   - Podman

     ```shell
     podman run \
       --detach \
       --name 'container-runtime-hardening' \
       --read-only \
       --read-only-tmpfs=false \
       --cap-drop=ALL \
       --security-opt=no-new-privileges \
       --memory=512m \
       --tmpfs /tmp:rw,nosuid,nodev,size=128m,mode=1777 \
       --volume "$(cat './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'):/diagnostics:nocopy" \
       --publish 8080:8080 \
       --env 'JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS=-Xmx256m -XX:StartFlightRecording=name=demo,settings=default,maxsize=32m' \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root'
     ```

4. Wait for the quote endpoint, then fetch a quote.

   Polling is bounded. A startup failure prints the container logs instead of
   waiting indefinitely.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote. A JSON response confirms that the packaged service is
   running and can serve its endpoint.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Abraham Lincoln",
     "id": 2,
     "quote": "I am a slow walker, but I never walk back."
   }
   ```

5. Inspect the restrictions configured for the running container.

   Read the container configuration to verify that it specifies the intended
   user, a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities and
   `no-new-privileges`. This checks the settings recorded by the container
   engine; the following commands check the process identity and write access.

   ```shell
   docker inspect 'container-runtime-hardening' \
     --format 'user={{.Config.User}} read-only={{.HostConfig.ReadonlyRootfs}} cap-drop={{json .HostConfig.CapDrop}} security-options={{json .HostConfig.SecurityOpt}}'
   ```

   The configuration specifies user `10001:10001`, a read-only root filesystem,
   dropped capabilities `ALL` and the `no-new-privileges` security option.

   ```
   user=10001:10001 read-only=true cap-drop=["CAP_CHOWN","CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE","CAP_FOWNER","CAP_FSETID","CAP_KILL","CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE","CAP_SETFCAP","CAP_SETGID","CAP_SETPCAP","CAP_SETUID","CAP_SYS_CHROOT"] security-options=["no-new-privileges"]
   ```

   Verify the effective identity of a process inside the running container.
   Execute `id` without overriding the user. This confirms that commands started
   in this container use the intended non-root identity, rather than relying
   solely on the configuration reported by `inspect`.

   ```shell
   docker exec 'container-runtime-hardening' id
   ```

   The process reports UID 10001 and GID 10001, matching the configured non-root
   identity.

   ```
   uid=10001(10001) gid=10001(10001) groups=10001(10001)
   ```

   Verify that the non-root user can write to the explicit temporary mount.
   Create a file under `/tmp` to confirm that the writable mount has suitable
   permissions. The read-only root filesystem should prevent writes to image
   directories while still allowing the temporary writes the application needs.

   ```shell
   docker exec 'container-runtime-hardening' sh \
     -c 'touch /tmp/workshop-write-test && echo "Explicit temporary write succeeded"'
   ```

   The success message appears only if the file write succeeds, confirming that
   UID 10001 can write to the explicitly mounted `/tmp` directory.

   ```
   Explicit temporary write succeeded
   ```

6. Verify that the application directory remains read-only, even for root.

   Root is used only for this inspection command to distinguish a read-only
   mount from an ordinary file-permission denial. The Java process keeps its
   non-root identity. The expected exit code is 1.

   ```shell
   docker exec --user 0:0 'container-runtime-hardening' \
     touch '/opt/app/workshop-write-test' 2>&1
   ```

   Providing writable mounts has not made the packaged application directory
   writable.

   ```
   touch: cannot touch '/opt/app/workshop-write-test': Read-only file system
   ```

### Preserve diagnostic evidence

A container can serve requests successfully while still being unable to save
useful evidence. Verify the diagnostic path too. The JFR repository uses
temporary storage, while the exported recording goes to the persistent volume.

1. Dump the active recording into the diagnostic volume.

   `jcmd` runs as the same effective user and group as Java. The exec-form
   entrypoint makes Java PID 1, and `/tmp` remains available for the JVM attach
   mechanism.

   ```shell
   docker exec 'container-runtime-hardening' \
     jcmd 1 JFR.dump name=demo filename=/diagnostics/demo.jfr
   ```

   The JVM writes the recording into `/diagnostics` rather than the read-only
   application directory.

   ```
   1:
   Dumped recording "demo", 1.2 MB written to:

   /diagnostics/demo.jfr
   ```

   Wait a couple of seconds for the dump to complete.

   ```shell
   sleep 5
   ```

   Verify that the file was created

   ```shell
   docker exec 'container-runtime-hardening' test -s '/diagnostics/demo.jfr'
   ```

2. Stop and remove the application container.

   Removing the container discards its temporary mount. The named volume
   remains. Saving the recording explicitly before stopping also avoids relying
   on a dump during shutdown, which cannot complete after a forced kill.

   ```shell
   docker stop --time 20 'container-runtime-hardening'
   docker rm 'container-runtime-hardening'
   ```

3. Inspect the saved recording after removing the application container.

   Start a temporary container and run `jfr summary` instead of the Java
   application. Mount the same diagnostic volume at `/diagnostics` so the tool
   can read `demo.jfr`. A successful summary confirms that the recording remains
   accessible and readable after the application container has been removed.

   Keep both the root filesystem and the diagnostic volume read-only. The volume
   needs its own read-only option because `--read-only` applies to the root
   filesystem, not separately mounted volumes. This container only needs to
   inspect the evidence, so it should not have permission to modify it.

   Use the command for your container engine. Docker uses `--mount` with
   `readonly` and `volume-nocopy`; Podman uses `--volume` with `:ro,nocopy`.
   Both mount the volume read-only and prevent copying the image directory into
   it. Podman also uses `--read-only-tmpfs=false` to disable its automatic
   writable temporary mounts, which this inspection does not need.

   - Docker

     ```shell
     docker run \
       --rm \
       --read-only \
       --entrypoint jfr \
       --mount "type=volume,source=$(cat './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'),target=/diagnostics,volume-nocopy,readonly" \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
       summary /diagnostics/demo.jfr
     ```

   - Podman

     ```shell
     podman run \
       --rm \
       --read-only \
       --read-only-tmpfs=false \
       --entrypoint jfr \
       --volume "$(cat './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'):/diagnostics:ro,nocopy" \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
       summary /diagnostics/demo.jfr
     ```

     The JFR summary reports the recording duration and event counts, confirming
     that the saved file can be read after removal of the application container.

     ```
      Version: 2.1
      Chunks: 1
      Start: 2077-04-27 12:34:56 (UTC)
      Duration: 5 s

      Event Type                              Count  Size (bytes)
     =============================================================
      jdk.TenuringDistribution                 1665         17112
      jdk.ActiveSetting                         752         19066
      jdk.ObjectAllocationSample                506          7547
      jdk.BooleanFlag                           494         14642
     ...
     ```

4. Export the recording to the host before removing the volume.

   Start a temporary container that reads `/diagnostics/demo.jfr` using `cat`.
   The shell running the command redirects those bytes into `target/demo.jfr` on
   the host, preserving the recording for analysis after the volume is removed.

   Use the variant for your container engine. Docker mounts the volume using
   `--mount` with `readonly` and `volume-nocopy`; Podman uses `--volume` with
   `:ro,nocopy`. Both provide read-only access without copying image contents
   into the volume. Podman also disables its automatic writable temporary mounts
   with `--read-only-tmpfs=false`.

   The exported file is build output, so a subsequent `mvn clean` removes it.

   - Docker

     ```shell
     docker run \
       --rm \
       --read-only \
       --entrypoint cat \
       --mount "type=volume,source=$(cat './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'),target=/diagnostics,volume-nocopy,readonly" \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
       '/diagnostics/demo.jfr' > './target/demo.jfr'
     ```

   - Podman

     ```shell
     podman run \
       --rm \
       --read-only \
       --read-only-tmpfs=false \
       --entrypoint cat \
       --volume "$(cat './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'):/diagnostics:ro,nocopy" \
       'container-runtime-hardening-spring-boot:non-root' \
       '/diagnostics/demo.jfr' > './target/demo.jfr'
     ```

   Verify that the exported file exists and is non-empty. `test -s` produces no
   output on success and returns a non-zero exit status if the check fails.

   ```shell
   test -s './target/demo.jfr'
   ```

Heap dumps and fatal-error logs need the same deliberate path decision.
Configure `-XX:HeapDumpPath=/diagnostics` when enabling heap dumps and
`-XX:ErrorFile=/diagnostics/hs_err_pid%p.log` for fatal-error logs. Those files
can be large or contain sensitive data. Provision appropriate capacity, access
and retention. This walkthrough creates a JFR recording rather than deliberately
crashing the application or exhausting its memory.

### Clean up

1. Remove only the volume created by this walkthrough and the local
   runtime-state files. The image and exported recording remain available for
   inspection.

   ```shell
   docker volume rm "$(cat './target/diagnostics-volume.txt')"
   rm -f './target/diagnostics-volume.txt'
   ```

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- Non-root execution, file ownership and a read-only root filesystem apply
  complementary restrictions. Writable mounts still need suitable permissions.
- Temporary files need explicit writable storage. A bounded tmpfs consumes
  memory and disappears when the container stops.
- Diagnostic evidence needs a writable path and a retention plan. The recording
  in this example survives container removal because it is saved to a Docker
  volume.
- The same image runs with different deployment settings. Verify application
  behaviour and diagnostics under the restrictions you actually deploy.
